claims.text: Rapid SPS consolidation will produce W38Ta36Cr15V11 with an initially uniform nanocrystalline structure.
A roughly 5-minute SPS dwell at 1100 °C limits the time available for Cr and V diffusion and clustering.
Rapid cooling after SPS reduces the formation of pre-irradiation solute clusters.
The proposed processing route will leave fewer pre-existing solute clusters than conventional SPS.
Pre-existing Cr/V-rich solute clusters act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for irradiation-induced Cr/V precipitation.
A post-SPS stress-relief anneal will reduce residual non-equilibrium defects.
Residual non-equilibrium defects provide nucleation sites for segregation or precipitation.
Combining ultra-fast SPS, rapid cooling, and stress-relief annealing will suppress radiation-induced Cr/V precipitation.
At approximately 8 dpa, the processed material will have at least about 30% less Cr/V precipitation than the conventional-SPS control.
The proposed processing route will permit efficient irradiation-defect recombination.
Efficient defect recombination will reduce the population of surviving irradiation defects responsible for hardening.
The processed alloy will exhibit less than a 15% irradiation-induced increase in nanohardness.
Suppressing precipitation while retaining efficient defect recombination will preserve negligible irradiation hardening.
SPS can consolidate powder into a fine-grained, controlled, high-density material using short soaking times and high heating and cooling rates.
The proposed SPS route will improve the alloy's suitability for practical bulk fabrication.
The precipitation-suppression mechanism is applicable to energetic-particle irradiation up to approximately 8 dpa at temperatures below 800 °C.
Approximately 1100 °C and a roughly 5-minute dwell constitute an applicable SPS processing window for the proposed effect.
Rapid cooling must be optimized to avoid excessive residual stress.
